nodes.title: Working with the specification
nodes.text: How the specification is kept and implemented.

children.title: The model
children.text: What the specification is made of and how it is changed.

children.title: The nodes are the specification
children.text:
The specification is the set of its nodes.

Whatever is generated from them — a readable export (for example, in markdown), the map, the instructions an agent reads — is regenerated after every change to them and never edited, and nothing is ever read back from it into the specification. What is generated from them into the system's code, its types and runtime checks (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9), waits for its nodes instead: it is regenerated only once every node it is generated from is checked, and until then no commit changes it.

Where a generated copy is kept, it is checked against what the nodes produce, unless it waits.
children.rationale:
A structure a schema can check is hard for a person to read, so a readable copy is needed; but a copy that is edited, fed back into the nodes or left behind them would be a second version of the rules: sooner or later one version would change and the other not, and whoever read the unchanged one would implement a rule that no longer holds. Regenerated by the tools at every change and checked against the nodes, a copy is a view of the one source rather than a second one.

Code generated from a node is part of the system: regenerated from a node not yet checked, it would implement what the node's owner has not confirmed (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug). Waiting, it lets a change to the node be committed before its confirmation, as a change to any rule is; and since no commit changes it meanwhile, it is still never edited. A copy that waits is left behind its nodes only until every one of them is confirmed, and its lag is reported meanwhile (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh), so that nobody takes it for current.

decisions.problem: A changed data record node could not be committed before its confirmation, since its commit passed neither with the generated types left behind it nor with new ones naming an unchecked node, while a rule could; and regenerating code from an unchecked node implemented what its owner had not confirmed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: code generated from the nodes follows only checked nodes; while one it is generated from is unchecked, it stays as it was and its lag is reported, not refused.

children.title: The structure of the specification is defined by its schema
children.text: The structure of every node and every file of the specification is defined by its schema. A file that does not match the schema is refused, and the refusal names the field that is wrong. Why each part of the structure is as it is, is written in the schema beside it.
children.rationale: A structure stated in prose can be broken without anyone noticing; stated as a schema that every file is checked against, it cannot. The schema is therefore the only description of the structure, and a rule that names a part of it, to say what that part means, is compared with it by machine.

decisions.problem: The rule named the files the schema is kept in, which is the layout of one toolset rather than what the specification requires.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the guidelines apply the split between base and appendix to themselves (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8); where the schema is kept is described in the appendix of the tools.

children.title: A node is one rule, and a section holds rules
children.text: One numbered rule is one node, and its continuation paragraphs, tables and code blocks belong to that node rather than standing beside it. A section is a container of rules: its text states what the section is responsible for and requires nothing, since every requirement is a rule, and it holds at least one rule — a data record node or a term node counts as one, and the rules of the sections inside it count as its own. A section whose rules have all gone is deleted, and every link and citation naming it is moved to the node that now holds its matter, or removed.
children.rationale: A rule's parts only make sense together. Splitting them into nodes of their own would invent a second address space for fragments nothing can cite. A requirement written into a section's text is a rule nobody can cite, tag or check on its own, and a section with no rule states a responsibility nothing in the code answers to. A data record node and a term node each state on their own what must hold, as a rule does — a data record the shape of its data, a term what its word means in every rule that uses it — and each is cited and tagged by its sid, so a section holding one holds a requirement.

decisions.problem: The check of a checked section counted a data record node and a term node as its rules, while this rule named rules alone, so a section of terms, such as a glossary of contracts, passed the check and broke the rule as written.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record node and a term node count as rules of their section; that terms are not duplicated is held by contracts alone holding them and by no two of them sharing a name.

children.title: A node is cited by its sid, and its id is its address
children.text:
A node carries a sid, given to it once and never changed, and is cited by it everywhere: in the links between nodes, in the code, in the tests and in commits.

Its id is its address: the part it stands in, followed by its place there — for a section or a rule, its number among the sections and rules under the same parent; for a term, the term. The header of a domain is addressed by the domain's name alone, and the node at the top of a file of the guidelines, of the technical appendix or of contracts by the part's name and the file's; each file of the guidelines and of the appendix is numbered under that address of its own, while contracts, like a domain, is numbered under the part's name straight through its files.

The address is computed from where the node stands, never written by hand, and nothing refers to it.
children.rationale: A reference to a place breaks whenever the place changes, and a specification that grows is reordered and has its rules moved between domains for as long as it grows. A sid is not a place, so a move cannot break a reference that holds it: moving a node changes its address, never its sid. The address stays where a person reads, computed so that it can never disagree with where the node stands.

decisions.problem: A test in a language whose names cannot hold a hyphen declares its sid by a mark rather than in its name.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a sid is cited in the tests, however a test declares it (§s-rwqzepmrt77rv35).

children.title: Checked means its owner confirmed its present wording
children.text:
A node's status is empty or checked. Checked means that the node's owner (§s-67vekyup7y8smap) confirmed its present wording — its title, text and reason, and the values its kind carries beside them, such as the fields of a data record node.

Any change to that wording, the owner's own included, leaves the node unchecked until its owner confirms the new wording, and so does a move or a change that gives it another owner. So does a withdrawal of its confirmation, which anyone may make, outside the SpecSheriff guidelines a project takes (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), and which names whoever made it.

A change to its links or its metadata leaves the status as it is.
children.rationale:
A checked status claims that the node's owner agreed to what it now states. A status that survived a rewrite would certify words nobody confirmed, and one that survived a change of owner would certify them in the name of someone who never agreed to them.

Links and metadata are not what an owner confirmed, and they change as the specification grows around a rule.

A withdrawal gives no agreement in anyone's name: it only leaves a node unchecked, as a change to its wording by anyone does, so whoever finds a confirmed rule wrong can keep any further change to its code or its tests from being committed (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug) without waiting for its owner; naming them tells the owner whom to ask.

decisions.problem: A data record node holds its fields apart from its text (s-e877bnfa559tvk9), and a field changed would have left the status standing over a structure the owner never confirmed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record node's fields are part of the wording a confirmation covers.

decisions.problem: A kind of node came to carry values beside its text, and a value changed would have left the status standing over values the owner never confirmed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the values a node's kind carries beside its text are part of the wording a confirmation covers, as a data record node's fields are.

decisions.problem: One person confirmed every node, and the values a confirmation covered were listed by the kinds of node one project uses.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an owner of the part a node stands in confirms it (§s-67vekyup7y8smap), and a confirmation covers whatever values the node's kind carries beside its text. An owner's own change to a wording needs a new confirmation as anyone else's does, since the fingerprint of the wording, not who changed it, decides.

decisions.problem: A move was said to leave the status as it is, while only a node's owner confirms it, so a node moved under another owner stood checked over words that owner never read.
decisions.ruling: The owner: checked means the node's owner confirmed its present wording; a move or a change that gives the node another owner empties its status.

decisions.problem: The reason held that a checked status claims its owner read the words a node holds, while a node may now be confirmed in its owner's name where its change states nothing new.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-67vekyup7y8smap: a checked status claims the owner agreed to what the node states.

decisions.problem: No rule said who may withdraw a confirmation, while the procedure let anyone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: anyone may withdraw a confirmation, and the withdrawal names whoever made it; the SpecSheriff guidelines a project takes stay as they were confirmed where they are written (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab).

children.title: Only its owner confirms a node
children.text:
The specification has one owner. A domain (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7) or a section may have an owner of its own, who takes the place of the owner above for every node within it.

A node is confirmed by its owner and by nobody else, and a confirmation names the owner. The exception is a node whose wording changes only to state what its owner confirmed in another node, or only by a replacement that changes no meaning, such as a renamed term or path: the agent that made the change, working for that owner, confirms it in the owner's name, as the owner's confirmation, and reports it to the owner, who may withdraw it.
children.rationale:
A confirmation means that whoever answers for a rule has agreed to what it states, so it is that person's to give. Owners of domains and sections divide the reading as the specification is divided, so that it can grow beyond what one person reads.

A node whose wording only states what its owner confirmed in another node asks nothing its owner has not agreed to, and a replacement that changes no meaning states nothing new; shown again, either would spend the owner's attention on no decision. An agent working for the owner already acts in the owner's name and reports to the owner as it works: the report lets the owner see that the change was only that, and withdraw the confirmation where it was not.

decisions.problem: One owner confirmed every node, which binds a growing specification to one person, and the confirmations were kept outside the specification, where nobody else could check them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a domain may name its owners in its header; a confirmation names who gave it, beside the fingerprint of the wording, is kept with the specification and is accepted only under that owner's signature. A confirmation read off the approvals of a merge request was declined, since it would tie what a status means to one hosting platform.

decisions.problem: Owners could be named on a domain's header alone, and a confirmation was to carry its owner's signature, made with a key no agent can use.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the specification has one owner, and a domain or a section may have its own, taken as a task is taken, oneself included; a confirmation names its owner and carries no signature, the agent's hooks guarding the status.

decisions.problem: The spec-review skill had the agent confirm, unshown, a node changed only to state what its owner had confirmed in another node, or by a replacement changing no meaning, while this rule let nobody but the owner confirm a node.
decisions.ruling: The owner: such a node is confirmed in its owner's name by the agent that made the change for that owner, which reports the confirmation to the owner; the owner may withdraw it. The owner amended the principle that nothing unconfirmed is implemented to the same effect.

children.title: An unchecked node is not implemented
children.text: A node is implemented only once it is checked. Before a domain's implementation begins, the domain is reviewed whole; where the implementation then finds a node silent or wrong, that node is changed and reviewed when the problem is found, not later.
children.rationale: The specification is expected to be incomplete. Implementing an unchecked node fills its gap with a guess made in the code, which the specification then does not hold; reviewing the node at once keeps the answer in the specification.

children.title: Removal goes through the archive when the node was ever confirmed
children.text:
A node a confirmation was ever given for is moved to the archive when it is removed, together with the reason for its removal and the sid of the node that replaces it, if one does. A node never confirmed is deleted outright, whatever cited it.

A node may later be deleted from the archive.
children.rationale:
A rule its owner confirmed is one the code may implement, and a later change to its wording does not undo what was implemented from it, so its removal is worth keeping for a time. Kept in its last wording, it can be restored if its removal is undone. And it is a record for the decisions taken: a confirmed rule that had to go, a rule of the base above all, most often shows a logic or an approach that was mistaken, which later work has to understand and take into account, as it would a list of the defects found.

Nothing guarantees how long the archive keeps a node, so a link or a citation naming an archived node breaks when the node is deleted, and the checks refuse it until it is removed. A node never confirmed was never implemented, since no tag may name it, and archived it would only bury the rules that had to go under wording nobody confirmed.

decisions.problem: The reason spoke of the specification's owner, while a confirmation is now given by an owner of the node's part.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an owner of the node's part (§s-67vekyup7y8smap).

decisions.problem: The reason held that the archive keeps resolvable the citations in the code, the tests and the commits that implemented a removed rule, while nothing keeps a node in the archive for good.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the archive keeps a removed node for a time, so that it can be restored and so that later work learns from what was found wrong, as from a list of the defects found; a node may be deleted from it, and a link into it may then break.

children.title: A decision lives on the rule it settled
children.text: A decision records what was settled about a rule. It is kept in that rule's metadata, never as a document of its own. A decision usually changes the rule's wording; a procedural one changes none.
children.rationale: A decision is not specification but the history of one rule, and it is read beside that rule. The procedural kind would otherwise leave no trace, because nothing in the wording shows it. And the number of decisions on one rule measures how well it was written: a rule that keeps collecting them was written badly.

children.title: A rule and its reason are held apart
children.text: A node's text states what must hold, except a rule of the technical debt, which describes a problem as it stands (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw). Why it must hold is kept in a separate field of the same node and is not part of the requirement. When a rule is revised, its reason is checked first: a rule whose reason no longer holds is removed, not reworded.
children.rationale: Mixed in one text, a rule is long and a reviewer cannot tell which half is being asserted. And a reason that has stopped holding is the surest sign the rule should go — which nobody sees while the reason is buried inside the requirement.

decisions.problem: A rule of the technical debt describes a problem as it stands and states nothing that must hold, which this rule did not admit.
decisions.ruling: Carried from the owner's ruling of the same day on the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw): the exception is written here, where the rule it narrows is read.

children.title: What the specification governs
children.text: The specification describes the system — its logic, its architecture and everything the system is made of — and governs one process only: how the specification itself is kept, changed and implemented. A rule that tries to govern anything else is dropped, and so is a rule that states the obvious.
children.rationale: A rule governing what nobody here controls decides nothing: an agent that has never read an instruction cannot be stopped by it, however many are written. Duplication and drift are fought by structure — one model, a generated export, links a checker resolves — not by prohibitions. A rule stating the obvious costs a reading and decides nothing either.

children.title: The specification holds its content; the code implements it
children.text: The specification holds its content and the code implements it, never the reverse. A rule does not hand what it states to a declaration in the code: a set of states, a list of members, a table of routes is described in the specification, and the code is checked against it. A rule that sends its reader to a source file for its content is a defect, repaired when that rule is revised.
children.rationale: A specification that leaves a list in the code and names only its meaning cannot say what the system is, and a copy of that list written beside it in prose goes stale with nothing noticing. Held in the specification and checked against the code, the content is in one place and the disagreement is found by a machine.

children.title: The base specification names no technology
children.text: A rule of the base specification states what the system does, never how the default implementation does it: it names no programming language, library, store, protocol, command or file path. How it is done, and any part of a rule that depends on it, is described in the technical appendix. A technology may be named by example, in brackets, where the rule does not depend on it.
children.rationale: The same rules can then be implemented on another stack, with an appendix of its own, without editing a single rule; and a rule that names its tools goes stale when they change, although what the system does has not.

decisions.problem: One rule held what the base names of a technology, of a look and of one instance, and grew too long to read as one requirement.
decisions.ruling: The owner: three rules, one for each.

children.title: Of a user interface the base states what it shows, not how it looks
children.text: Of a user interface, the base specification states what a user can rely on in any instance: what is shown, what it means, in what order, in which states, and what the user can do. How it looks and is built — placement, size, colour, icon, the kind of control, where a state is kept — is described in the technical appendix.
children.rationale: The same rules can then be given another look with an appendix of its own; and a rule that names its look goes stale when the look changes, although what the user can rely on has not.

decisions.problem: Nothing said whether the look of a user interface belongs in a rule of the base specification, and rules named column widths, where the browser keeps them and the icons of a menu.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the base specification holds what a user can rely on in any instance — what is shown, what it means, its order, its states, what can be done; the technical appendix holds how it looks and is built — placement, sizes, colours, icons, the kind of control, where a state is kept. A menu's order and nesting stay in the base, its icons go to the appendix.

decisions.problem: The rule carried an exception for a menu generated from the specification, which not every project has, and named the person using an interface by one project's term.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project needing such an exception writes it into its own guidelines, refining this rule (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab); the rule speaks of a user.

children.title: The base specification holds no figure of one instance
children.text: The base specification holds no figure measured on an instance — a population, a rate, a duration observed there. A threshold a rule needs is stated by the method an instance measures it with, and its value is a setting of the technical appendix.
children.rationale: A figure belongs to the instance it was measured on and to the day it was measured, so every other instance would pass or fail the rule by accident.

decisions.problem: A rule of the writing doctrine forbade numbers measured on a running instance, written to repair rules into which one instance's data had leaked.
decisions.ruling: The owner: in a specification written fresh it is one case of the base being tied to no implementation, and stands beside the rules on technology and on a look.

children.title: The technical appendix stands beside the base specification
children.text:
The technical appendix describes how this repository builds the system — its stack, how each domain is built and how the user interface looks — in the detail an instance needs to repeat it; every part but it and the guidelines is the base specification.

It is no domain and stands at no level, beside the domains as contracts does, with a section for each domain it implements, under that domain's name, one for the stack, and, while any problem is set aside, one for its technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

It never contradicts a rule of the base specification but extends and refines it: a rule too narrow for an implementation is widened in the base, its detail going to the technical appendix.

A node of the appendix describes how the nodes of the base specification it implements are to be carried out, in enough detail to be read only one way — exact values, examples and the edge cases of that implementation — and never restates what they state. Each of its nodes but a section, which requires nothing (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg), implements at least one node of the base specification, except a choice covering the whole system, which stands in the section of the stack, and except the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

An instance changes the technical appendix for itself, and what instances vary within it is a setting, described with its default.
children.rationale:
The base specification stays stable while an implementation adapts to an instance's infrastructure and requirements, so only the technical appendix changes with an instance.

A part allowed to contradict the base would leave the base binding nowhere, since no rule could be relied on without reading the implementation too. Read beside the nodes it implements, an appendix node restating them would be a second copy, and a copy drifts from what it copies; how a rule is carried out has no other home, since the base names no technology, and described less exactly it would leave a choice to whoever implements it, which the code would then hold and the specification would not.

It is no subject area of the system but the way every one of them is built, which no level can place. A node bound to the rule it implements is found when that rule changes and is read beside it, and divided as the base is, the implementation of a rule is looked for in one place.

The problems set aside are read as one list, so they stand in one section, which spans the domains as the stack does, and a problem is not how a rule is carried out but where carrying it out falls short.

The repository holds nothing of any one instance, so what one instance chooses within the appendix is a setting, not a rule.

decisions.problem: The technical appendix had no stated place beside the domains, nothing said whether it could depart from the base specification, and its nodes were bound to no rule they implement.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the technical appendix stands outside the levels, as contracts does; it never contradicts the base specification but extends and refines it, a rule too narrow being widened in the base; every node implements a node of the base, the choices of the stack excepted; it is divided as the base is; this repository's appendix is the default implementation, an example each instance changes for itself, and it keeps its name, its being the default a detail.

decisions.problem: Nothing said what a node of the technical appendix holds beside the nodes it implements, and a draft retold the base rule it implemented while the values of its implementation had been moved into code.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node of the appendix describes how the base nodes it implements are carried out, in enough detail to be read only one way — exact values, examples and edge cases — and never restates them, its links carrying what they state; the base answers what is done, the appendix how. Values taken from the code and a running instance while a project's existing documents are brought into the model are a departure recorded in the guide to adopting the method, not in the guidelines.

decisions.problem: The specification had no place for a problem of the implementation the owner set aside, so such a problem waited in the list of tasks as a task nobody meant to do.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the technical appendix holds a technical debt, one list of the problems of the implementation set aside, each only described as it stands; its standing there is the decision to set it aside.

decisions.problem: The rule had each node of the technical appendix implement a node of the base, its sections included, while a section requires nothing and the appendix's sections stand under the names of the domains they implement.
decisions.ruling: Following §s-7445ahgjck2aefg: a section of the technical appendix implements nothing; it stands under the name of the domain it implements.

children.title: The technical debt holds the problems of the default implementation set aside
children.text: The section of the technical debt holds rules alone, each describing one problem of the default implementation as it stands and refining the nodes the default implementation falls short of there, one of the base specification at least; where the problem lies in a technology the default implementation uses, its rule names the version of that technology it was seen in. Standing there is the whole of the decision to set the problem aside: its rule carries no reason, no decision records it, and the change that solves the problem removes the rule.
children.rationale: A problem set aside needs a place where it is stated, or it is forgotten, or kept as a task nobody means to do. Every problem there stands for the one reason that the specification's owner judged it not worth solving now, so a reason or a decision of its own would only repeat its standing. Described as it stands and bound to the nodes it concerns, it tells whoever repeats an instance, or reads those nodes, what the implementation does not do; a problem in a technology may be solved by a later version of it while nothing here changes, and the version it was seen in lets a reader tell. Left standing once solved, it would describe a shortfall that no longer exists.

children.title: The guidelines hold their base and the appendix of their tools
children.text: The guidelines are divided as the specification is: their base states what is held, what is checked, when, and what a failure costs, and names no technology; the appendix of the tools describes how one toolset carries that base out — its commands, its hooks, where it keeps the files, how it reads code and who runs its reviewer. Each rule of that appendix implements at least one node of the base. The appendix of the tools is not the technical appendix, which describes how the system is built and never the tools of the specification.
children.rationale: The guidelines require of every base specification that it name no technology (§s-5x737t9nee4zgaa) and are held to it themselves: a rule naming its tool goes stale when the tool changes, and another toolset, written in another language, could not implement it. The tools hold the specification and the code to each other rather than make up the system, which is why they are described apart from the technical appendix. Bound to the node of the base it implements, a rule of the appendix is found when that node changes.

decisions.problem: The guidelines named the commands, the hooks, the files and the parser of the tools that check them, which their own rule forbids a base specification to do.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the guidelines apply the split between base and appendix to themselves, so that another toolset can implement the same base.

children.title: A project's own guidelines refine or implement the SpecSheriff guidelines
children.text: The guidelines are the SpecSheriff guidelines and a part each project holds as its own: the base of the SpecSheriff guidelines, which every project shares, with the appendix of the toolset the project uses; and the project's own guidelines, which hold what only its specification needs, such as the specification's owner or the list of levels its domains stand at. Each rule of a project's own guidelines refines or implements a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines and never contradicts it. A project holds no copy of the SpecSheriff guidelines: they come whole with the skills that apply them and are updated with them, and are changed only where they are written.
children.rationale:
The SpecSheriff guidelines, shared by every project, are what lets a tool, a skill or a reader carry from one project to the next, and a project needs what they cannot foresee. Refining or implementing the SpecSheriff guidelines and never contradicting them, a project's own rules extend them as the technical appendix extends the base, so that a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines can be relied on in every project without reading that project's own.

Coming whole with the skills, the SpecSheriff guidelines read the same in every project working by one release, and stand confirmed there as they were confirmed where they are written; a copy changed in one project would be a second version nobody who writes them reads.

decisions.problem: Rules only one project's specification needed stood in the guidelines every project would share.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the SpecSheriff guidelines hold what every project shares; a project holds what only its specification needs as rules of its own, standing to them as the technical appendix stands to the base.

decisions.problem: The SpecSheriff guidelines were to name owners of their own, as a domain does, so that the confirmations they carried into a project would hold there under signatures that project's owner never gave.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the SpecSheriff guidelines are no domain and have no owners in a project; a project takes them whole, at a version its specification's owner names, their confirmations stay where they are written, and the checks compare them to that version.

decisions.problem: The part of the guidelines every project takes whole was named the core, a general word that does not say of what.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it is named the SpecSheriff guidelines.

decisions.problem: Whether a project names the version of the checks it runs, taking the tools of that version from the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in into a cache on the machine, or the plugin, which Claude Code updates on each machine, carries the tools.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the plugin is a package holding everything its work needs, and every release reaches every machine through the marketplace's update; a machine not yet updated is its user's matter, and a team's CI is its own and left out of the design.

decisions.problem: Whether a project's own guidelines may hold rules tied to no rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines, provided they contradict none.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every rule of a project's own guidelines refines or implements a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines. The link is what lets a reader judge that it contradicts none, which no check can decide, and a rule on keeping the specification that finds no parent there is most likely a rule of the product.

decisions.problem: The rule let a project's own guidelines hold a kind of node of its own, while the schema every project reads admits only the kinds it defines.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-rah8b37kytb682y: the kinds of node are those the schema defines (§s-eferktypcj7njt5), the same in every project.

children.title: Data structures are described in the specification
children.text:
A data record the domains pass to one another or keep in a store is described by a node of its own, a data record node: its name, what it is, each of its fields with its type in neutral terms, a whole number's or a number's with any bounds on its value, whether it is required and what it says, what happens to a field nobody declared, and, where another data record refers to it by an identifier, the field that identifies it. The rules that bind one field to another are rules linked to the data record.

The implementation's types and its checks of data at runtime are generated from the data record nodes and never written beside them; which mechanism performs the checks is described in the technical appendix.
children.rationale: Written beside the description, a type or a check is a second copy of the same structure and drifts from it; generated, the two cannot disagree. A structure is part of what the system is, so it belongs in the specification rather than in the code. The bounds a value may take are part of its type. An identifier of a data record has the type of the field that identifies it, so that field is named where the data record is described.

decisions.problem: A data record node could not say which values a number field may take, so the bounds of a setting were stated by no node while two components each checked them by hand.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the bounds go into the field's type, named as JSON Schema names them, and the check is generated from them, over writing them in the field's words or dropping them.

decisions.problem: The rule had every value choosing a form be a form, so a value carrying nothing got a form holding nothing, and it did not say when a field is required, so values that may not come were required; worded in one long rule, it was hard to read.
decisions.ruling: The owner: base data, set beforehand or made by the system, is required; additional data is required where its case guarantees it and optional otherwise; a form exists only where a value carries fields of its own. The rule is divided: this one keeps what a data record node holds and that types are generated from it, and three rules of their own say when a field is required, when a value has a form, and where each value choosing a form is declared.

decisions.problem: No node could hold a data record's structure, and a data record whose body differs with its kind had no way to be described at all.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record is described by a node of its own, with its fields; a data record whose fields depend on its kind holds the fields common to every kind and those its kind brings.

decisions.problem: Nothing said what type an identifier of a data record has, and nothing named the field that identifies a data record.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an identifier has the type of the field that identifies the data record it names, which that data record's node names.

children.title: A field is required only where its value is guaranteed
children.text: A field is required where every data record that can hold it has its value: the value is set before the data record is written, the system makes or observes it whenever it writes the data record, or the system refuses to write the data record without it, as what identifies the data record. Every other field is optional: one whose value only some data records, or some moments of a data record, have, or one an answer the system reads may not carry.
children.rationale: A value that may not come cannot be demanded: demanded, it is invented to fill the field, or a data record that should have been written is refused for want of it.

decisions.problem: Nothing said when a field of a data record is required, so values that may not come were declared required, and a value carrying nothing was given a form holding nothing.
decisions.ruling: The owner: formal fields, set beforehand or made by the system, are required; additional fields are required where their case guarantees them, as an identifier an external system gives a data record that cannot exist without it, and optional otherwise, as an external system's answer.

children.title: A data record variant exists only for a value carrying fields of its own
children.text: Where a data record's fields depend on the values of some of its own fields, the data record names those fields as choosing its variant. A value that brings fields of its own has a data record variant: a data record node in the part of the specification declaring that value — a domain, or contracts — which refines the data record, names the values it answers to and declares those fields. A value that brings none has no variant, and a data record holding it holds only the data record's own fields.
children.rationale: A variant holding nothing says nothing the declaration of its value does not, so it would be a second copy of that declaration. A variant is held by the part of the specification declaring its value, so that part adds a variant without changing the data record or the variants another part holds.

decisions.problem: Every value choosing a data record's form had a form, so a value carrying nothing got a form holding nothing; and form, a general word, named both a data record's shape and what a user fills in on a page.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a value carrying no field of its own has no form, which was a crutch; and the data record's form is named data record variant, a form staying what a user fills in.

decisions.problem: Nothing limited a data record to one field of type variant, and with two it is left unsaid which of them holds the fields of the chosen variant.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record holds at most one field of type variant, which its schema checks. Fields that do not depend on the variant are the data record's own, or the fields its field of type variant holds whatever the variant; two independent choices are two data records, each choosing its own variant.

decisions.problem: A data record in contracts may name fields choosing its variant, and a value its field's own list declares is then declared in contracts, which is not a domain, so no variant could stand where this rule placed it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a variant stands in the part of the specification declaring its value, a domain or contracts, as the tools already held it.

children.title: Each value choosing a data record variant is declared once
children.text: Each value of a field choosing a data record variant is declared once, whether or not a variant answers to it. It is declared either in the field's own list of values, or, for a data record described in contracts, in a list defined in a rule of a domain, which refines that data record and names the field whose values its list declares.
children.rationale:
Declared once, a value is checked against every variant naming it, and a variant naming a value nobody declared is refused rather than read as a value of its own; a value with no variant is declared too, since the field may hold it all the same.

A data record described in contracts is shared by domains, so a domain adds the values it brings, and the variants answering to them, in a rule of its own, without changing the data record, which the owner of contracts holds; a data record one domain provides is described in that domain (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3), which declares its values itself.

The list names its field because a data record may choose its variant by several fields, and it refines the data record by its sid, so that it stays bound to the data record through a rename, and the check that each value is declared once follows that link.

decisions.problem: The values choosing a data record's variant were read off its variants alone, so a value without one had to be given a variant holding nothing, and values declared in a sentence no tool can read were checked against no variant.
decisions.ruling: The owner: each value is declared once, in a place a tool reads, whether or not a variant answers to it.

decisions.problem: The rule named, beside a field's own list of values, the tables one project's tools read such values from.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the SpecSheriff guidelines keep the field's own list, and a project's own guidelines may declare such values elsewhere (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab).

decisions.problem: The rule allowed a place a project's own guidelines name for a variant's values, and nothing described how they name it, so the tools read the field's own list alone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the other place stays and is described. For a data record described in contracts, a rule of a domain defines a list of the field's values and refines the data record by its sid; the tools collect the values from every such list and refuse one declared twice, the variant stands where its value is declared, and the generated types list every value. A data record one domain provides keeps its values in its own field, as the rule on contracts requires.

children.title: What the domains share is agreed in contracts
children.text: Contracts is not a domain: it belongs to none of them and agrees what they share and how they work together — the terminology, the conventions every domain's API follows, and the rules that bind more than one domain. A domain coins no term of its own — a term it needs is added to contracts — and a term is defined once: one term naming two things, or two terms naming one, is refused. What only one domain needs, it holds itself. A data record one domain provides to others is described in that domain, as part of its interface; contracts describes a data record only where no single domain provides it, as a store more than one domain writes.
children.rationale: Domains that coin their own words, or their own conventions for the same exchange, stop understanding one another, and a reader cannot tell whether two words mean one thing. Holding in contracts only what binds more than one domain keeps it from owning what a single domain defines. A data record described away from the domain that provides it has no owner: the provider changes what it gives while its description stands elsewhere.

children.title: The specification is divided into domains
children.text: The specification is divided into domains. A domain of the specification is the part of it devoted to one subject area of the system: it has its own responsibility. The guidelines and the technical appendix are not domains.

children.title: A part of the specification can be read alone
children.text: Each domain, contracts, the technical appendix and the guidelines are held apart, and a part too large to read at once is divided into one file per section.
children.rationale: The specification is too large to fit whole into the context window of an agent working with it. It is therefore divided into self-contained domains, and a domain into sections, so that only the part the work at hand needs is loaded. Contracts is the exception: shared by every domain, it is loaded whichever part the work needs.

children.title: An entity is declared once
children.text: Every entity of the system — what a term names, such as a user or a session — is declared once: by the term that names it, in contracts (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3), and its data, where the specification describes them, by one data record node, standing in the domain that provides it or, where no single domain does, in contracts. No two data record nodes share a name.
children.rationale: Two definitions of one entity are two owners of it, and two owners change it apart; the duplicate is usually the first visible trace of one domain doing another's work.

children.title: A domain's specification opens with its header
children.text: A domain's specification opens with its header: a node stating what the domain does, its owner where it names one (§s-67vekyup7y8smap), the level it stands at and where its code is, whose consumes links name the sections of other domains the domain uses. The header also carries the index of the domain's sections — each one's sid, title and text, the text of a section stating what that section is responsible for, and the domains that use it — built from the sections and never written by hand.
children.rationale: Whoever works on one domain loads its header and learns from it alone what the domain is responsible for, who answers for its wording, how it is divided and what it takes from the others, without loading the rest. The index is built rather than written, because a table of contents kept by hand is a second copy of the sections and drifts from them.

decisions.problem: The owners of a domain had nowhere to be named.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the header names them (§s-67vekyup7y8smap).

decisions.problem: Whether a domain may leave its header out, and whether a section has a header of its own, as a node of service carrying its metadata.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every domain opens with its header, which alone gives it its level, and so its place on the map and in the order of the domains; a section has none, since its own text says what it is responsible for and it names its own owner.

skills/tools/test/unit/reindex.test.ts::s-yggv9myedprnaa7 rebuilds the index in a domain's header from the domain's sections

children.title: Every domain stands at a level
children.text: Every domain stands at one of the levels the specification's owner lists in the project's own guidelines (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), from the general to the particular: the smaller a domain's responsibility, the lower its level. A level is always shown as its number and its name together, and its number is its place in that list.
children.rationale: The links between domains give an order but not a place: a domain that uses nothing may be where the others start or stand apart from them, and one that nothing uses may be where they end or stand over them. The level says which.

decisions.problem: The rule listed the levels one project's domains stand at, which another project's domains need not.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the SpecSheriff guidelines keep that every domain stands at a level, from the general to the particular; the list of levels is the project's, in its own guidelines (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab).

children.title: The order of the domains
children.text: The domains are ordered by the consumes links of their headers: a domain stands after every domain it uses and as close as possible before the domains that use it; where the links put two domains in the same place, they stand in the order of their names. The domains do not use one another in a cycle.
children.rationale: A domain cannot work without the domains it uses, so this is the order the domains are specified and built in, and computed from the links it cannot disagree with them. Standing as close as possible before its users, a domain is taken up when the first of them needs it. A cycle has no such order.

decisions.problem: The reason rested the refusal of a cycle on a rule outside the guidelines, which a project need not hold.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reason stands on the order alone, which a cycle cannot have.

decisions.problem: Whether domains using one another in a cycle should be refused or only reported, since domains link to one another across their lines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the cycle stays refused. It is read from the consumes links of the domains' headers alone, not from the links between their rules, which may cross domain lines freely; a cycle of consumes leaves no order to specify and build the domains in, and usually shows a part both share that belongs in contracts or in a domain below them.

children.title: Links
children.text: How one node of the specification bears on another.

children.title: Outgoing links are written, incoming links are built
children.text:
A node declares the links it makes, each naming the node it points at, and, for every other node it cites — `§` followed by that node's sid, in any of its fields but its links, the nodes under it and a header's index of its sections, outside a span quoted as code — at least one naming that node.

The links pointing at it stand in the same list, each naming the node it comes from and read from this node's end; they are rebuilt from those declarations — every such entry removed first and built again — and are never written by hand.

A node of the archive is held to neither: it holds no link pointing at it, and none it declares is built into another node.

A node of the SpecSheriff guidelines holds only the links pointing at it from the SpecSheriff guidelines.
children.rationale:
A reverse link kept by hand survives the removal of its other end and then reads as a live relation. Rebuilt from scratch every time, the reverse direction is correct whatever was skipped before. Held in one list with the links the node makes, they show every relation of the node from where it stands, the end each entry names telling the direction.

A citation relies on the node it names as a link does; with no link of its own it is seen only where it is written, and missed by whoever changes the node it names.

A node of the archive is no longer part of the specification, and a link built to or from it would read as a live relation.

The SpecSheriff guidelines read the same in every project working by one release (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), and a list in them of the links one project makes to them would hold true of that project alone.

decisions.problem: A citation in a node was only a candidate for a link whose type a review was to name, a step no rule stated and nobody took, until hundreds of citations named nodes their own node held no link to, and the nodes cited showed nobody citing them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: no candidates — a node citing another declares the link to it, of the type that says how the two bear on each other or cites, and the reindex builds the side pointing at the node cited as it does for every link; a citation with no link is refused, and the links the citations lacked are written once.

decisions.problem: A project's own guidelines refine or implement rules of the SpecSheriff guidelines, which a project reads from the plugin for Claude Code and never writes, so the links pointing at those rules could not be held there; and where the SpecSheriff guidelines are written, the links its own project guidelines make would have been written into them and carried to every project.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project's links to the SpecSheriff guidelines are one-way, as a law lists no act made under it; links in both directions stay everywhere else, between the rules of a project's specification and the nodes implementing them.

decisions.problem: The links pointing at a node are built from the links the nodes make, so they could be computed whenever they are asked for rather than stored in the node.
decisions.ruling: The owner: they stay stored in the node, so that an agent opening a node sees what depends on it without remembering to ask.

children.title: A link carries its type
children.text:
Every link names what it means, as one of these types: implements — the linking node is how the linked one is carried out; refines — it states the linked node more precisely, or for a narrower case; constrains — it holds a condition the linked rule depends on; consumes — the domain whose header holds the link uses what the linked section of another domain provides; supersedes — it replaces the linked node, which is archived; exempts — a node of the project's own guidelines takes the linked rule, or every rule under the linked section, out of the rule that a checked rule is implemented (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf), for the reason its text gives; cites — the linking node cites the linked one (§s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz) and no other type says how the two bear on each other, so it holds no link of another type to it; term-relation — the linking term and the linked term are bound, for as long as both exist, in the ratio the link carries; uses — what the linking term names makes use of what the linked term names while taking part in a process, as a user fills in a form while signing up, and the link carries no ratio; a term that only starts a process, as an operator starting an export, uses nothing the process uses.

A term-relation and a uses link bind two terms, and no other type does, cites included: a term citing another term holds a term-relation or a uses link to it.

A ratio is the multiplicity of each end in the usual notation, 1, 0..1, 1..N or 0..N, the linking term's end first — user 1:0..N session says that a user has any number of sessions and that a session belongs to exactly one user. Read from the linked term, the ratio is reversed.
children.rationale:
A link without a type records only that somebody thought of two nodes together: no check can grade it and no diagram can draw it. A type named without its meaning is the same guess one step later.

A citation is typed by the words around it where no name of a type says more, so its link has a type of its own rather than none. A use is kept apart from a term-relation because making use of something does not last and has no number to it: given a ratio, it states a multiplicity nobody means. A term that only starts a process takes no part in it, so a use of what the process uses would claim a part it never takes.

An exemption is a link rather than a mark on the exempted rule, so that one node gives the reason for every rule it exempts, and each exempted rule outside the SpecSheriff guidelines shows, among its incoming links, what exempts it.

list.of: the types a link between nodes of the specification can carry

decisions.problem: A person fills in a form another term builds, and no ratio fitted that relation: it lasts only while the form is filled, and a term-relation states a multiplicity that holds for as long as both terms exist.
decisions.ruling: A second type of link between terms, uses, carrying no ratio; a term-relation is bound for as long as both terms exist.

decisions.problem: A person only starting a process was nearly linked to what that process uses, as if taking part in it.
decisions.ruling: A uses link is for a term taking part in a process; one that only starts it uses nothing the process uses.

decisions.problem: A form of a data record refines the data record (s-e877bnfa559tvk9), and refines was defined over rules alone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: one word changes, rule to node — a form of a data record is the data record for a narrower case; a longer definition was declined as padding.

decisions.problem: A link declared for a citation had no type to take where none of the types said how the two nodes bear on each other, which left the citation a candidate for a link nobody typed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: such a link has a type of its own, cites, standing only where no other type describes the two nodes.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

decisions.problem: No type of link could take a rule out of the rule that a checked rule is implemented.
decisions.ruling: The owner: exempts, from a node of a project's own guidelines to a rule or a section.

children.title: A link may cross a domain line
children.text: A link between nodes of the specification may cross a domain line: a rule of one domain may point at a rule of another, and the link carries its type like any other. Whoever would point at a statement of another domain that no node there holds first gives it to a node of that domain that can carry it, or, failing one, writes a rule there whose todos name the node linking to it, and links to that node.
children.rationale: Domains build on one another — a later one uses what an earlier one provides — and the specification has to be able to say so. A link holds the sid of the node it points at, so moving either node leaves it whole, and a link to a node that no longer exists is refused by the checker the same day. A statement named in words rather than by a node is a reference no check can follow, and the node it means shows nobody relying on it; given to a node there it keeps one home, and a rule written for a link is read when its domain is, its todo saying why it stands there.

decisions.problem: The citation check refused a citation crossing a domain line unless it named a node of a few domains, a list the tool kept and no rule stated, and such citations had been replaced by the words of the rule they named; that a citation into another domain names a node there stood nowhere.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a link of any type, cites among them, crosses a domain line freely and is checked only for naming a node, over admitting one only into what the linking domain's header consumes; a statement no node of the other domain holds is given to a node there, or a rule is written there for the link.

children.title: Code
children.text: How the code implements the specification and the tests verify it.

children.title: Code changes only as a consequence of the specification
children.text: Behaviour changes by changing the specification first; the change to the code follows from it. Every commit that changes code names, by its sid, each checked node whose implementation it adds or changes — one whose text has just changed, or an existing one the code contradicted — and every tag on a symbol it adds or changes names a node the message names, or is the tag that names none. The message names no domain's header and no section.
children.rationale: Wanting different behaviour is a reason to change the specification, not the code. A commit that repairs code which contradicted the specification as it stood is the same procedure and not an exception to it: there the specification was already right. The message and the tags name the same nodes so that the message says which nodes the commit serves, and a header or a section is refused because it requires nothing a change could serve.

decisions.problem: A commit changing a domain's code named the domain's header, which says nothing of what the commit changed, and the check of the message accepted it, since any node that exists was accepted.
decisions.ruling: The owner: code changes only through the specification. A commit names the checked rules it serves, the tags of the declarations it changes name those rules, and a header or a section never stands in for a rule.

children.title: Three records, each answering a different question
children.text: A rule is bound to its implementation by three records: a tag carrying the node's sid, on the symbol in the code that implements it; the node's sid declared by the test that verifies it, so that a run of the tests reports it; and, in the node's metadata, the lists of that code and those tests. All three are written by hand, and they must agree.
children.rationale: Each answers a different question. The tag says what a symbol implements. The sid a test declares says whether the rule is verified, so that a run of the tests is itself a report of which rules are covered. The lists say what implements a rule, to a reader who has the rule open.

decisions.problem: A test bound to its rule by the opening of its name cannot be written in a language whose names cannot hold a hyphen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a test declares the sid of what it verifies however its language allows, so that a run of the tests reports it.

children.title: The test comes before the code
children.text:
When a rule is implemented, its test is written first and the code that implements it second, written to pass that test. The test carries the rule's sid in its name, or, in a language whose names cannot hold one, in a mark on the test (§s-rwqzepmrt77rv35); the code carries the rule's tag (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4).

Every test carries the sid of the rule or the term it verifies. A test a commit adds or changes carries the sid of a checked one, and every rule whose code a commit adds or changes has at least one test.
children.rationale:
A test names a rule's behaviour, which survives the refactoring that moves and renames the code underneath it, so the binding through tests is the stable one. And a test written first tests the rule, not whatever the code happened to do.

A term whose definition states behaviour is verified as a rule is, and its test carries the term's own sid rather than that of a rule written only to repeat it. A section and a domain's header require nothing (§s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr), and what a data record requires is carried out by the types and runtime checks generated from it (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9), which every commit holds to what the node produces, so a test of its own would verify the generator rather than the system's code.

A test without the sid of what it verifies tests something nobody can name, and a rule whose code has no test is carried out on trust; both are refused where the change is made, which is when a test costs least to write. Only a test a commit adds or changes must name a checked node, since a rule under revision is unchecked while the tests written against its earlier wording still stand.

decisions.problem: Two tests added with a feature opened with no sid, and nothing checked that a test of the system's code names the rule it verifies.
decisions.ruling: The owner: tags and tests that cite the specification are the general rule for all code, checked at every commit.

decisions.problem: Tests of what a term of contracts defines opened with the term's sid, which the rule as worded refused.

children.title: Every symbol carries a tag, and what carries no rule says so
children.text:
Every symbol of the system's code — a function, a class or a member of one, a type, a constant, a component — carries a tag naming the node it implements, wherever in the code it stands and whichever domain the node belongs to; a symbol inside another is covered by the tag of the one it stands in.

A symbol that implements none of the system's logic but is required by the technology the system is built with — a framework, a library, the infrastructure — such as a module's re-exports or the glue a library needs, carries instead a tag that names no node and gives its reason.

The repository's tools, its configuration and its tests are exempt by where they live.

Only a symbol whose code a commit changes must name a checked node. A change to its tags is a change to its code; rewording the rest of its comments, moving a citation onto another sid or renaming an identifier everywhere it is spelled changes no code.
children.rationale:
A tag on every symbol is what makes logic without a rule visible: a symbol left untagged until somebody changes it hides until then whether any rule asks for it, one tag per file lets every symbol added to it later go untraced, and a binding read by the domain a file stands in misses code that implements another domain's rule.

Code that serves the stack exists because of how the system is built, not because of what it does, so there is no rule for it to cite; demanding one teaches people to attach whichever id is nearest, and marking it explicitly keeps 'nobody tagged it' apart from 'there is nothing to tag'.

Only a symbol whose code changes must name a checked node, since a rule under revision is unchecked while the code written against its earlier wording still stands, and a comment reworded, a citation moved or a name changed everywhere it is spelled changes nothing the code does. A tag counts as code because it decides which node the code is held to: were a change to it not counted, a tag could be moved onto an unchecked node, or onto one the code does not implement, with nothing refusing it.

decisions.problem: One tag per changed file was owed, and only in a domain with a checked rule of its own, so code implementing two checked rules of another domain shipped with no tag, and logic no rule stated passed beside it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: code changes only through the specification and never the reverse, enforced by scripts that refuse logic without a reference back to the specification and by an independent reviewer; every declaration a commit adds or changes carries a tag, in every domain and in contracts.

decisions.problem: A tag was owed only by a declaration a commit added or changed, so code nobody had touched since the rules were written stayed untagged, and whether a rule asked for it could not be seen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every declaration always carries a tag; a project adopting the method tags its code before the check is turned on.

children.title: A checked rule is implemented or exempted
children.text:
Every checked rule is implemented: a symbol of the system's code carries its tag, and a test carries its sid and passes. A tag or a test naming a rule that implements it, directly or through rules that implement those in turn, counts for it.

This holds for every rule of the specification but those of the SpecSheriff guidelines, of the project's own guidelines and of the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

A node of the project's own guidelines exempts a rule from being implemented through an exempts link to the rule, or to a section it stands under (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm), and gives the reason in its own text.
children.rationale:
A checked rule states what holds of the system it specifies, what the system does or how it is built, so one the system's code does not carry out leaves the specification stating what does not hold of it. A tag shows where the code carries the rule out (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4), and a test naming the rule shows that the code does what the rule says, but only while it passes, as every test of the system's code must before a commit is shared (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh); only both together show it by a check. A tag or a test of a rule implementing it counts, since an implementing rule is how the rule it implements is carried out (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm).

The SpecSheriff guidelines are carried out by the tools and the skills that apply them, never by code a tag binds: a project does not hold that code, and the repository writing them exempts it from tags by where it lives (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4). A project's own guidelines, which hold what only its specification needs (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), are carried out by those tools and skills and by people, not by the system's code; and a rule of the technical debt describes a problem set aside, which is not required of the system and goes once it is solved (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw). A rule the system's code cannot carry out, or that no test can verify, would be reported for as long as it stands, so it is exempted; the exemption is a node, which its owner confirms with its reason.

decisions.problem: Nothing reported a checked rule that the system's code did not carry out: a test was required only once a commit changed a rule's code, so a rule nobody reached stood unnoticed while the specification stated it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every checked rule is implemented — a symbol of the system's code tagged with it and a passing test carrying its sid, a tag or a test of a rule implementing it counting — or is exempted by a node of the project's own guidelines with an exempts link; the SpecSheriff guidelines, the project's own guidelines and the technical debt are outside it, where the guidelines are written as well.

children.title: The map
children.text: How the specification is drawn.

children.title: The map is a mindmap of the specification
children.text: The map is the specification seen from above: a mindmap drawn from the nodes each time it is built, holding no fact of its own. It shows the structure and nothing else — a domain, the parts under it, then the rules, down to the individual rule — from the nesting, the titles and the level of each domain alone. A branch opens and closes, so a reader goes to the part they came for while the whole stays in view around it. The branches read: the guidelines first, then contracts, then a branch for each level of the domains, from the top, holding its domains in the order §s-uw9n84edf7cbe9n gives, and the technical appendix last.
children.rationale: A specification is read one rule at a time and has to be understood as a whole, and the two pull against each other: the full text is more than anyone holds at once, and an extract loses where the rule sits. A mindmap answers both — the shape of everything, and the detail of whatever is opened. Drawn from the nodes at each build rather than kept beside them, because a diagram kept apart is a second copy of the specification and disagrees with it silently. The levels and the order of the domains carry how the domains bear on one another.
