children.title: The checks and the procedures
children.text: How a change to the specification or the code is checked, and how a procedure that writes the specification behaves.

children.title: What is checked, when, and what a failure costs
children.text:
Two things are checked mechanically: that the specification holds together on its own, and that the specification and the code still describe each other. Every check is deterministic but one: whether the code does what the nodes it names say, and nothing they do not, is judged at every commit that changes code by an independent reviewer (§s-nyh9yk22ba6g77q). The checks run when a commit is made, and the tests of the system's code before a commit is shared; each check reads the commit being made, and the history behind it where its row says so, never what the commit does not hold. A check refuses unless its row says otherwise.

**The specification on its own**

| What is checked | On failure |
|---|---|
| No file of the specification, of its archive or of its schema gives one field two values | refused |
| Every file matches its schema | refused |
| No two nodes share a sid | refused |
| No two nodes share an id | refused |
| Every node's id is the address its place gives | refused |
| Every term node stands in contracts | refused |
| No two term nodes name the same term, whatever the case of its letters | refused |
| No two data record nodes share a name, whatever the case of its letters | refused |
| A node outside the SpecSheriff guidelines a project takes is checked only where a confirmation holds the fingerprint of its wording and names the node's owner | refused |
| A node a commit removes, outside the SpecSheriff guidelines a project takes, is deleted where no confirmation of it was ever given, and otherwise stands in the archive with the reason for its removal | refused |
| Every link names a node | refused |
| A node citing another holds a link to it, and a link of type cites stands only where its node cites the node it names and holds no link of another type to it | refused |
| No node cites another by its address | refused |
| A term-relation or a uses link binds two terms, and no other type of link, cites included, binds two terms | refused, and settled with the specification's owner |
| The incoming links are what the outgoing ones produce | refused |
| No checked node sets three words or more running in capitals outside a name quoted from the code | refused |
| A checked section holds at least one rule | refused |
| Every domain has a header, and the index in it is what the domain's sections produce | refused |
| Every domain's header names a level the project's own guidelines list | refused |
| A consumes link goes from a domain's header to a section of another domain | refused |
| An exempts link goes from a node of the project's own guidelines to a rule or a section | refused |
| The domains do not use one another in a cycle | refused |
| A data record variant refines the data record it is a variant of | refused |
| A data record variant stands in the part of the specification that declares the value it answers to | refused |
| A data record variant declares at least one field held neither by its data record nor by any field of type variant of that data record | refused |
| A data record variant answers to values of exactly the fields its data record names as choosing the variant, each value declared in its choosing field's own list of values or in a list a domain defines for that field | refused |
| No two variants of one data record answer to the same values | refused |
| Each value of a field choosing a data record variant is declared once | refused |
| A list declaring values of a field choosing a data record variant stands in a rule of a domain, which refines a data record described in contracts naming that field as choosing its variant | refused |
| A data record holds at most one field of type variant, the ones it inherits counted | refused |
| Every field of type one of holds at least one value, in its own list or in a list a domain defines for it | refused |
| A field of type identifier of names a data record that names the field identifying it, one of its fields, and the identifying fields it leads to, followed from one identifier to the next, end in a field of another type | refused |
| Every node of the technical appendix but a section, outside the sections of the stack and of the technical debt, implements a node of the base specification, and every rule of the technical debt refines one | refused |
| Every section of the technical appendix but those of the stack and of the technical debt stands under the name of a domain | refused |
| Every rule of the appendix of the tools (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8) implements a node of the base of the guidelines | refused |
| Every rule of a project's own guidelines refines or implements a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines | refused |
| No project but the one the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in holds a copy of them or of their schema | refused |

**The specification and the code**

| What is checked | On failure |
|---|---|
| Every symbol of the system's code carries a tag naming the node it implements, or, where it implements none of the system's logic, the tag that says so and gives its reason | refused |
| Every tag names a node that exists, and a tag on a symbol whose code a commit changes a checked one | refused |
| Every tag stands on the symbol it binds | refused |
| Every test of the system's code carries the sid of a rule or a term that exists, and a test a commit adds or changes the sid of a checked one | refused |
| Every rule whose code a commit adds or changes has a test carrying its sid | refused |
| A node's lists of code and tests are what the tags and the sids the tests carry produce | refused |
| A node that names the symbols in a file is held to them | refused |
| A list a node carries matches the declaration in the code or in the schema it names | refused |
| No file the repository keeps outside the specification and its tools names a node by its address | refused |
| A citation in the code, the tests and the documents names a node by its sid | refused |
| Every copy generated from the nodes and kept in the repository, such as the types and runtime checks of the system's code, is exactly what the nodes produce now, or, while it waits for a node not yet checked, left unchanged by the commit: neither edited by hand nor left behind nodes that are all checked | refused |
| A copy of the system's code that waits for a node not yet checked | reported by the node's sid |
| A rule whose text has changed since its code last changed, as the history of the repository shows | reported by the node's sid |
| A checked rule outside the SpecSheriff guidelines, the project's own guidelines and the technical debt has a symbol carrying its tag and a test carrying its sid, its own or those of a rule implementing it, or is exempted | reported by the node's sid |
| A commit that changes code names every checked node its changed symbols' tags name, and no header or section | refused |
| The code does what the nodes it names say, and nothing they do not | refused, naming the node and the line |
| The tests of the system's code pass | the commit is not shared |
children.rationale:
A person asking whether a commit will go through must find the whole answer in one place: spread across several rules, the answer comes apart, and one rule ends up contradicting another without anybody seeing it.

Every check but the review is binary, so refusing costs nobody a judgement, and a check that sometimes refuses for a reason nobody can reproduce is bypassed at the first chance and never trusted again. The review is the one judgement, because whether code does only what its rules say cannot be decided by a script.

A check reads the commit being made, because a judgement of anything else would pass or refuse what is not being committed. The tests run before a commit is shared rather than when it is made, since a suite takes longer than a commit should wait, and a commit not yet shared misleads nobody.

The check of drift only reports, because a rule outrunning its code is drift worth knowing about and not the fault of whoever's commit found it. A checked rule not implemented is reported rather than refused, since a rule is checked before its test and its code are written (§s-rah8b37kytb682y).

decisions.problem: No check held the code to what its rules say: that was left to a review run on purpose, and none was run, so logic no rule stated reached a domain beside code that cited two checked rules.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every change to the code meets every requirement of the specification, checked at every commit by a separate, independent reviewer and by scripts that refuse logic with no reference back to the specification.

decisions.problem: The row refused a test opening with a term's sid, which §s-rah8b37kytb682y now admits, and read a test as changed where a deleted neighbour lent it the diff's lines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a changed test opens with the sid of a checked rule or term, and a test is changed when its text is.

decisions.problem: The data record nodes, and the code generated from them, had no check.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the checks of the specification hold a variant of a data record to its data record and its values to the fields that choose the variant; the binding holds the generated code to what the data record nodes produce.

decisions.problem: The checks of a data record's forms let a form hold nothing and read the values choosing a form off the forms alone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record variant declares a field of its own and answers to a value declared once.

decisions.problem: The check of the appendix's implements links would have refused every rule of the technical debt, which falls short of the nodes it concerns rather than carrying them out, and debt named the binding's report of a rule outrunning its code as well.
decisions.ruling: Carried from the owner's ruling of the same day on the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw): the debt's rules are held to a refines link to a node of the base and its section to none, and the binding's report is named the drift, the word this rule's reason already used, so that debt names one thing.

decisions.problem: The table named the commands and the hooks of one toolset, and held rows only one project's specification needed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the base keeps what is checked and what a failure costs; how, and by which command, is described in the appendix of the tools (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8), and a project's own rows stand in its own guidelines.

decisions.problem: Read row by row, the table left checks unclear or unmade: a term could stand in a domain with nothing refusing it, names differing only in case passed as two terms or two data records, two abbreviations side by side were refused as stress, one row joined five checks of a data record variant, and several rows named a thing without its object or read as cut off.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a term stands only in contracts; terms and data records are named once whatever the case of their letters; capitals are refused from three words running; the checks of a data record variant stand one to a row; and the rows on the appendix of the tools, the tags, addresses, generated copies and drift say what they check in full.

decisions.problem: A field of type one of could hold no value at all, and identifiers could lead from one identifying field to the next back to a data record already passed; neither has a type the implementation can be given, and nothing refused them.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's rulings of that day on where the values of a field of type one of are declared and on the type of an identifier: both are refused.

decisions.problem: The row let a test carry the sid of any node that exists.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-rah8b37kytb682y: a test carries the sid of a rule or a term.

decisions.problem: Nothing reported a checked rule that the system's code did not carry out, and no row held where an exempts link may stand.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's rulings on §s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf and §s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm: a checked rule neither implemented nor exempted is reported and refuses nothing; an exempts link goes from a node of the project's own guidelines to a rule or a section.

decisions.problem: The row held every node of the technical appendix to implement a node of the base, its sections included, and no row held a section of the appendix to the name of a domain.
decisions.ruling: Following §s-vj7ercem526zd6v: a section of the technical appendix implements nothing and stands under the name of a domain.

decisions.problem: The row held every kept generated copy to what the nodes produce now, while code generated from the nodes now waits for them to be checked.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j: code generated from the nodes waits until every node it is generated from is checked, no commit changing it meanwhile, and its lag is reported.

children.title: The reviewer sees only the change and the nodes it names
children.text: The independent reviewer of a commit is given the commit's change, less the files generated from the specification, and the text of the nodes its message and tags name, a data record with its fields — and nothing of the session that wrote the code. It refuses the commit where the code does something no named node states or leaves out what one requires, and names the node and the line of each finding. A review that cannot be held — no reviewer to run, a run that does not end, an answer that cannot be read — refuses the commit and says why.
children.rationale: Given nothing of the session that wrote the code, the reviewer reads the code against the nodes rather than against its author's intent, and a refusal naming the node and the line can be checked by anyone. The generated files are left out because the binding check already compares them with what the nodes produce. A review that passes whenever it could not be held is a review nobody can rely on.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was given the rules a commit names and no data record, so code generated from a data record had nothing to be read against, and the definition of a term the code's names follow was withheld; a generated data record was refused field by field as stated by no rule.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reviewer is given the rules, data records and terms the message and the tags name, a data record with its fields.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was one agent's command line, so the method read as one vendor's tool, and a reader without that agent could not run it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the base states the reviewer's contract; who carries the review out is a runner described in the appendix of the tools, and a review that cannot be held refuses the commit.

children.title: A procedure that writes the specification is idempotent
children.text: Every procedure that writes the specification, or what is generated from it, is idempotent: run again on what its previous run left, it gives the same result and changes nothing, so running it again is always safe. A procedure needed only once, such as bringing existing documents into the model, is removed once it is done, since it is idempotent only on the state of the specification it was written for.
children.rationale: Whoever works on the specification may run such a procedure at any time, by hand or as part of a check, without knowing whether it has run before; one whose second run changed anything would damage the specification the next time it ran. A procedure written for one state of the specification can damage a later one.

decisions.problem: Safety to run again was stated of the commands of one toolset, in words that did not name the property they meant.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it is stated of every procedure that writes the specification, by its standard name, idempotent.

children.title: Where an agent writes, the checks run at each of its edits
children.text:
Where an agent writes the specification, the tests or the code, the checks of the specification and of the code run after each of its edits, and what they refuse is reported to the agent.

Before an edit is made, it is refused where it would leave a node checked over a wording its owner never confirmed (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq), change the code of a rule no test carries the sid of (§s-rah8b37kytb682y), or change the confirmations otherwise than through the procedure that records a confirmation or withdraws one.
children.rationale:
An agent told of a refusal at the edit that caused it mends it there, rather than at the commit among every other.

A node is confirmed by its owner, or in the owner's name by the agent working for that owner where its change states nothing new (§s-67vekyup7y8smap), so an agent that could set a status, or write a confirmation itself, could confirm what its owner never agreed to; and every later check takes the confirmations as given, so they can be held only where they are written. The procedure that records a confirmation takes the wording the node already holds and refuses a node whose owner is someone else, and a withdrawal only leaves a node unchecked.

A commit holds a test and its code together whichever was written first, so the order of the work can be held only where the edits are made.

decisions.problem: The checks ran only at a commit: an agent met every refusal at once, far from the edits that caused them, nothing held the order of rule, test and code that a commit cannot show, and a status an agent set was caught only at the commit.
decisions.ruling: The owner: where an agent writes, the checks run at each of its edits, and an edit that would leave a node checked unconfirmed or change the code of a rule with no test is refused before it is made; the hooks ship with the tools and are kept in git.

decisions.problem: An agent could write a confirmation of a new wording into the confirmations and then reword a checked node: the check before the edit found the confirmation and let the edit pass, and only this rule's reason spoke against it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an agent's edit changing the confirmations is refused before it is made; only the procedure that records a confirmation or withdraws one writes them.

decisions.problem: The reason held that nobody but a node's owner confirms it, while the agent working for the owner may now confirm in the owner's name a node whose change states nothing new.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-67vekyup7y8smap: the reason names that exception.

children.title: How a rule is written
children.text: How a node of the specification is written.

children.title: The specification is written in English
children.text: Every node of the specification is written in English, and so is everything generated from the nodes. A quotation, such as a name from the code or a text the system shows its users, keeps the language of what it quotes.
children.rationale:
A specification that mixes two languages, in its nodes or in what is generated from them and read in their place, loses the line between what it states and what is an aside.

The language is English because a project's guidelines include the SpecSheriff guidelines, which a project takes as they are written and never changes (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), and those are written in English: a project's own nodes in another language would mix two languages in one specification. English is also the language the readers of a specification are likeliest to share.

A quotation must match what it quotes letter for letter, and, standing apart from the words around it, it does not blur what the node states.

decisions.problem: The rule named English, a choice one project made for its readers, which another project's readers need not share.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the specification is written in one language, English being recommended and holding where a project's own guidelines name no other; the SpecSheriff guidelines themselves are written in English.

decisions.problem: The rule let a project's owner name another language for the specification and required everything generated from its nodes to be in it, while a project's guidelines include the SpecSheriff guidelines, written in English, and no field held the language named for a tool to write in it the words it adds to what it generates, such as the labels of the export and of the map; and the one language held a node's quotations too, though a name from the code or a text the system shows its users may be in another.
decisions.ruling: The owner: everything of SpecSheriff is in English, every project's specification included; a quotation keeps the language of what it quotes.

children.title: A rule names its subject and states what must hold
children.text: A rule names the subject it binds and states what that subject must do: not “credentials are kept encrypted”, which binds nobody, but “the store of secrets keeps every credential encrypted”. A property is stated over what the specification declares, never over what happens not to exist yet: not “a timestamp needs no time zone while every user is in one”, but “a timestamp carries its time zone”. A rule of the technical debt names its subject the same way and states what that subject does while the problem stands (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).
children.rationale: Such a sentence is true when it is written and silently false afterwards: nothing breaks, no check can fire, and the next reader takes an observation for an obligation. Naming the subject is also what makes a rule gradeable at all, since a requirement with nobody to hold it is one nobody can be found to have broken. A rule of the technical debt describes on purpose, and is removed with its problem (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

decisions.problem: A rule of the technical debt states what its subject does while a problem stands, which this rule's demand that a rule state what its subject must do did not admit.
decisions.ruling: Carried from the owner's ruling of the same day on the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw): the exception is written here, where the rule it narrows is read.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

children.title: A name is quoted where the reader must reach it, a predicate where the rule must keep binding
children.text: Where a rule binds a named thing, the name is quoted where the reader must reach the definition that owns it, and the predicate is stated where the rule must keep binding if that name changes: not “`deleted_users` is never searched”, which binds nothing once the table is renamed, but “a table holding the users who deleted their accounts — today `deleted_users` — is never searched”.
children.rationale: A sentence written against a name goes inert rather than failing when the name moves: nothing breaks, no test moves, and a requirement quietly becomes a statement about nothing. A sentence written against the predicate keeps binding whatever the thing is called, and is useless exactly where the reader needs to find the definition.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

children.title: A reason is no narrower than the rule it holds up
children.text: A node's reason covers everything the node's text requires: a rule that refuses an upload too large to store and tells the user why gives a reason for both, not only for the refusal. Where the reason is narrower, either the reason is completed or the rule is cut back to what the reason carries.
children.rationale: A rule with a narrow reason is destroyed by the next author doing everything right: the change is checked against the stated reason, the reason still holds, and the property nobody wrote down is gone. A reviewer cannot defend what the node never said.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

children.title: A reason gives its grounds and nothing more
children.text: A reason states the ground its rule rests on, as a rule in its first sentence. Beyond that ground, a reason carries only a caveat for a case the ground does not reach, and further grounds that do not overlap it; what a mistake would cost and a restatement of the rule's text are left out.
children.rationale: Whatever a reason says beyond its grounds blurs them, until a reader can no longer tell which sentence the rule rests on. And a rule held up by grounds that do not overlap survives any one of them going stale.

children.title: No count in prose
children.text: A node states no count of what the specification or a registry holds — of nodes, of states, of members, of commands — and a sentence correcting a count is a count. Where the number matters, it is produced by whatever holds the set: not “contracts holds 45 nodes”, which was true for one day, but the figure counted off the model each time it is shown.
children.rationale: A count is a second copy of a fact, and the copy is the one that goes stale. It goes stale silently and in the direction that reads as correct, because a number that is merely out of date looks exactly like a number that is right.

children.title: A restriction by list is chosen by which mistake would go unnoticed
children.text: Where a rule restricts something by a list, it says whether the list names what is allowed or what is forbidden, and chooses by which mistake would go unnoticed: where something left out would go unnoticed, the list names what is forbidden, as the records a backup leaves out; where something let in would go unnoticed, it names what is allowed, as the fields a public API returns.
children.rationale: A list goes wrong on whatever nobody thought of when it was written: one naming what is allowed shuts out every newcomer, one naming what is forbidden lets every newcomer in, and for a given restriction only one of those two mistakes is noticed.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

decisions.problem: The rule spoke of sets, where what a rule does is restrict something by a list, and spent its words on what everyone knows of allow-lists and deny-lists rather than on how to choose between them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it speaks of a restriction by list and keeps the criterion for choosing one.

children.title: A general word carries its object
children.text: A rule names the concrete thing it means rather than a general word for it: not “a limit on how many records a listing shows”, which also let an export drop records, but “a limit on how many records a user interface shows”. Where a general word cannot be avoided — a model, a structure, a check — it carries its object in the same phrase: the structure of which record, the check at which moment comparing what with what, the model of what. A name the specification defines — a term, a data record, a field — is never a general word alone, such as type, action or item, but carries its object: userAction, not action.
children.rationale: A rule has no conversation around it to supply a missing object, and a general rule has the least context of all, so every reader supplies an object of their own and the rule binds whatever each of them chose. Nothing about the word itself looks wrong, which is why the ambiguity survives every reading. A defined name is read in every rule that uses it, far from its definition, and a general one there means whatever each rule's context suggests: a field called type held a kind of request in one log, a user's action in another and a kind of error in a third.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

decisions.problem: The schema of a node names several of its fields type and one kind, general words this rule keeps a name the specification defines from being.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a field of the node schema is read within the object holding it, which carries its object, so the schema keeps type and kind.

children.title: No phrase or sentence is set in capitals
children.text: A node is written in the ordinary case of its language, and a name quoted from the code keeps its spelling. Outside such a name, capitals may stand on one word or on two running (REST API); a phrase or a sentence, three words or more running, is never set in capitals: what must stand out is said in the words.
children.rationale: Set in capitals, a phrase reads as more binding than the words around it, although every word of a rule binds alike, and a reader who meets capitals on every line starts reading the capitals instead of the sentence. A style spreads by imitation, because a rule is written like the rules around it, so one rule in capitals is copied by its neighbours. A word or two in capitals are most often an abbreviation or a name keeping its own spelling, which no check tells from a word stressed, so they are left alone. Three words running are seldom anything but stress, and a run of abbreviations as long is rare enough to be worded around.

decisions.problem: The check refused two words in capitals running, so two abbreviations side by side, such as REST API, were refused as stress although this rule let an abbreviation keep its capitals; and a single word stressed in capitals, which this rule forbade, no check could tell from an abbreviation.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a single word, or two running, may stand in capitals; a phrase or a sentence, from three words running, never does.

children.title: What no rule requires is not done
children.text: Whatever no rule requires is not done, and needs no rule saying so. Where a rule's words would also cover a case they must not, the exception is written into that rule, so that the rule is exact where it is read.
children.rationale: A prohibition that answers no rule decides nothing, and each one written suggests that whatever it does not name is allowed. An exception kept apart from the rule it narrows is missed by whoever reads the rule alone.

decisions.problem: A rule binding every store of one kind fitted a store for which it had nothing worth measuring, and a rule saying only that something is not done had been proposed for it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: what no rule requires is understood as not done and needs no rule; an exception refining a general rule is written, for the rule to be exact.
